I am 55 and have worked these 11.6 mu for three decades. I never went to school, but I know this soil and the weather of Quzhou better than any book. My family has six mouths, and some of the younger ones have jobs in town, so I must be careful with labor. Cotton earns money, but it is a demanding crop—too much for me to handle alone if I plant too much. So this year I will put 3 mu into cotton, which I can manage with the help I have at home. The remaining 8 mu will stay in my wheat-maize rotation; that is the foundation of my farm and gives me both grain to sell and feed for the household. I keep 0.6 mu for mungbean because it does not need much fertilizer—being a legume, it makes its own nitrogen—and the beans are good for eating at home.

I have a well, so when the rain does not come, I can pump water. But pumping costs money and time, so I do not over-irrigate. For the winter wheat, I will give it three good waterings: one when it greens up in spring, one at jointing, and one during grain filling. For the summer maize, two irrigations are enough—at the big trumpet stage and when it tassels. Cotton needs water at seedling, flowering, and boll stages, so three times there as well. The mungbean only needs one watering when it flowers, if the soil is dry.

For seeds, I buy hybrid maize and hybrid cotton because they yield more and resist pests better. For wheat, I use an improved variety that does well here. For mungbean, I use my own seeds that I saved from last year—why spend money when they grow fine?

For fertilizer, I know what these crops need. Wheat gets about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus phosphate and potash. Maize takes about 15 kg of nitrogen. Cotton needs roughly 12 kg of nitrogen and a bit more potash because it is a fiber crop. Mungbean needs very little nitrogen—maybe 2 kg per mu—and some phosphate and potash.

I plough deeply before planting wheat and cotton because their roots need loose soil. For maize and mungbean, which come after wheat, I use the rotary tiller to save time and get them in the ground quickly before the summer heat sets in.

I spray pesticides when I see insects or disease, not just for the sake of it. Wheat and maize need about two applications each. Cotton is different—the bollworms and aphids never leave it alone, so I will spray five times. Mungbean usually stays fairly clean, so one spray is enough.

I expect my wheat to yield around 440 kg per mu, the maize about 530 kg per mu, the cotton around 240 kg per mu of seed cotton, and the mungbean about 65 kg per mu. These are honest numbers based on what this land has given me before.
